- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
IMPORTANT: WebFetch WILL FAIL for authenticated or private URLs. Before using this tool, check if the URL points to an authenticated service (e.g. Google Docs, Confluence, Jira, GitHub). If so, look for a specialized MCP tool that provides authenticated access.

- Fetches content from a specified URL and processes it using an AI model
- Takes a URL and a prompt as input
- Fetches the URL content, converts HTML to markdown
- Processes the content with the prompt using a small, fast model
- Returns the model's response about the content
- Use this tool when you need to retrieve and analyze web content

Usage notes:
  - IMPORTANT: If an MCP-provided web fetch tool is available, prefer using that tool instead of this one, as it may have fewer restrictions.
  - The URL must be a fully-formed valid URL
  - HTTP URLs will be automatically upgraded to HTTPS
  - localhost and other hostnames without a dot are not supported; for a local server, use curl via Bash
  - The prompt should describe what information you want to extract from the page
  - This tool is read-only and does not modify any files
  - Results may be summarized if the content is very large
  - Includes a self-cleaning cache (entries expire after 15 minutes) for faster responses when repeatedly accessing the same URL
  - When a URL redirects to a different host, the tool will inform you and provide the redirect URL in a special format. You should then make a new WebFetch request with the redirect URL to fetch the content.
  - For GitHub URLs, prefer using the gh CLI via Bash instead (e.g., gh pr view, gh issue view, gh api).

- Allows Claude to search the web and use the results to inform responses
- Provides up-to-date information for current events and recent data

  - The current month is (provided in the conversation below). You MUST use this year when searching for recent information, documentation, or current events.
  - Example: If the user asks for "latest React docs", search for "React documentation" with the current year, NOT last year

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

1	# AGENTS.md: Project 2 context for all agents
2	
3	Every agent (builder, reviewer, tester) reads this file first. Fill in the [TODO] parts before Step 0. Keep it short and specific.
4	
5	## Project goal
6	
7	Classify Android apps as malware or goodware from their API-call features, and find a sustainable approach that stays accurate as the data drifts over 8 years. The full assignment is in ASSIGNMENT.md.
8	
9	## Dataset
10	
11	- Location: input_data/ (not committed to git).
12	- The dataset files follow the naming scheme of "sampled_[year]_[class]_api.csv", where year is replaced with the year and class is replaced with either benign or malware "sampled_2014_benign_api.csv".
13	- Each file has 1,500 rows and 1,849 columns. The first column must be dropped; the other 1,848 columns are API-call features.
14	- Label: The model should label malware with the code "1" and benign or goodware as "0".
15	
16	## Folder layout
17	
18	- src/: project code (builder only).
19	- tests/: pytest tests test_stepN_*.py and test logs stepN_test_log.md (tester only; the student adds failure decisions).
20	- docs/: one builder report per step.
21	- reviews/: one review report per step (reviewer writes comments; student writes the decision log).
22	- transcripts/: saved agent sessions (saved by the harness; agents never edit these).
23	- PLAN.md: the plan for Steps 1-7. REPORT.md and REFLECTION.md: written by the student.
24	
25	## Coding conventions
26	
27	- Python 3, pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, scipy. No other libraries without asking.
28	- All code must be documented whenever new code is generated. Each method and class should have a docstring following the common format and information included, like a description, parameter values and explanations, and return values.
29	- Inside the method, code blocks should always have in-depth descriptors, labels, or explanations of the code unless it is trivial. The idea is that code reviewers should be able to quickly and easily understand what is happening.
30	- All code should be decoupled and modular. Code should follow typical standards and changing one thing should generally not cause more changes to occur whenever possible. 
31	- Code should not hard-code possible datasets or other information and should instead be determined at the time of running
32	- Train/test split is by year. Anything fit to data (scalers, feature selection, models) is fit on training years only.
33	- Malware is the positive class for precision, recall, and F1.
34	
35	## How to run
36	
37	- To run the project, enter the command python -m src.main
38	- Tests: python harness.py test N (one step) or python harness.py test all.
39	
40	## Commit rules
41	
42	Every commit message starts with a role tag: [builder], [reviewer], [tester], or [student]. A git hook rejects other messages. Make small commits, one per task. Never rewrite or squash history.
43

1	**Project 2: Classifying malware data and finding a sustainable ML approach with agentic AI coding**
2	
3	**Due Date:** Oct. 28 (Wed.) by 11:59 p.m.  
4	**Submission Format:** Individual  
5	**Required Approach:** Agentic AI coding with builder, reviewer, and tester agents
6	
7	For this project, you will implement two (or more) machine learning classifiers using scikit-learn. These classifiers will be applied to an Android malware dataset in the folder input_data.
8	
9	You must build this project with an agentic AI coding tool: an AI agent that plans the work, writes and edits files, runs code and tests, and fixes its own errors. Examples include Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Cursor in agent mode, and GitHub Copilot in agent mode.
10	
11	You will work with three separate agents, each with its own role: a builder agent that writes the code, a reviewer agent that reviews it, and a tester agent that writes and runs tests. Separating these roles means the code is checked by agents that do not share the builder’s assumptions, which is how agentic programming is done well in practice.
12	
13	Your role is the lead engineer. You give the agents context, set the direction, decide which review comments to act on, check results, and make the final decisions. You will be graded on both the results and how well you directed the agents, so keep a complete record of your process from the first session to the last.
14	
15	**Dataset**:
16	
17	The data consists of malware and goodware from Android apps over an 8-year period. The Android malware dataset has a property of data drift. Data drift occurs when the data used to train a machine-learning model is no longer representative of the new data the model encounters.
18	
19	Data drift refers to the change in the statistical properties of the data over time, which can cause a machine learning model’s predictions to become less accurate. It typically happens because:
20	
21	1.  **Feature Drift**: The distribution of individual features changes. For example, if you trained a model to predict sales based on seasonality, a sudden change in consumer behavior might impact your model's performance.
22	
23	2.  **Concept Drift**: The relationship between the input and output changes. For instance, a model predicting product demand might experience concept drift if the factors influencing demand evolve (like new trends or policies affecting consumer behavior).
24	
25	Detecting and addressing data drift is crucial to maintaining model accuracy over time. Common methods for managing data drift include monitoring model performance, retraining models on recent data, and utilizing adaptive algorithms that can adjust to changes in data distribution.
26	
27	The first column of each file should be discarded.
28	
29	Except for the first column, the information pertains to the API calls of Android apps.
30	
31	Each file has 1,500 rows and 1,849 columns.
32	
33	Target class: binary (malware and goodware)
34	
35	Labeling for target class: each file name includes the target class of each app in the file.

37	**Agentic AI Coding Requirements:**

39	1.  **Use three separate agents:** Run the builder, reviewer, and tester as separate agent sessions. The same tool and model may be used for all three (a different model is welcome but not required). Each must start with a fresh context: the reviewer and tester must never see the builder’s conversation. Name the tool and model for each role in your README.
40

42

It writes a review report in reviews/ (e.g., reviews/step1_review.md) listing problems such as bugs, data leakage between years, wrong metrics, and unclear code.

1	# PLAN.md
2	
3	Plan for Steps 1-7 of Project 2 (Android malware classification under data drift). Written by the builder agent in Step 0. All code lives in `src/`; each step also produces a report in `docs/` (templates already exist there) and is reviewed/tested by separate agents.
4	
5	## Train/test split by year and leakage prevention
6	
7	The dataset currently covers 8 years: 2014-2021 (one `sampled_<year>_benign_api.csv` and one `sampled_<year>_malware_api.csv` per year, in `input_data/`), but the exact years are never hard-coded in code or in this plan — they are discovered at runtime from `load_all_years` (Step 1) and the split is always computed relative to whatever years are discovered.
8	
9	- **Primary split (used for Steps 3-5):** `split_years_in_half(years: list[int]) -> tuple[list[int], list[int]]` (added to `src/preprocessing.py`) sorts the discovered years and returns `(train_years, test_years)` as the earlier half and later half (with the earlier half getting the extra year on an odd count). With the current 8 years this yields train = **2014-2017**, test = **2018-2021**, but the split follows automatically if years are added or removed from `input_data/`. This simulates a model trained once on historical data and deployed into the future, which is the realistic drift scenario the assignment asks about.
10	- **Per-year split (used for Steps 2, 6, and 7):** every year is also kept as its own labeled dataframe so drift can be measured year-to-year and performance can be reported year-by-year on the test years individually, not just on the pooled test set.
11	- **Leakage prevention:**
12	  - Any object that is *fit* (the `StandardScaler`, and the classifiers themselves) is fit only on rows from `train_years`. Test-year data is only ever passed through `.transform()` or `.predict()`, never `.fit()`.
13	  - Year boundaries are respected when concatenating: `split_by_year` (see Step 3) builds the train dataframe strictly from `train_years` and the test dataframe strictly from `test_years`; rows are never shuffled across that boundary before the split.
14	  - Drift statistics in Step 2 are descriptive (comparing year distributions to each other) and do not feed into any fitted object, so computing them does not leak test-year information into the model.
15	  - For Step 7 (sustainable approach), when a model is retrained on a later year, that year's data is added to the training pool *only after* it has first been used once as an unseen test year, so every year is scored by a model that has never seen it before being folded into training for subsequent years. The scaler is also refit from scratch on the current training pool before each retrain round (see Step 7), so it never sees the not-yet-scored year either.
16	  - No feature-selection step is used anywhere in the pipeline: with two classifiers that natively tolerate 1,848 features (L2-regularized Logistic Regression, and Random Forest's per-tree feature subsampling), feature selection is not needed for correctness, so there is nothing fit-to-data in this category to leak. If a later step found it necessary, it would be fit on `train_years` only, same as the scaler.
17	
18	## Step 1: Prepare the Data
19	
20	**Approach:** Read each `sampled_<year>_<class>_api.csv` file, drop its first column (an identifier, not a feature), attach a label parsed from the filename (`malware` -> 1, `benign` -> 0), and concatenate the two classes for each year into one dataframe per year. Years are discovered from the filenames present in `input_data/` rather than hard-coded, so the pipeline keeps working if years are added or removed.
21	
22	**Files and functions (`src/data_loader.py`):**
23	- `extract_label_from_filename(filename: str) -> int` — parses the class token (`benign`/`malware`) out of a filename like `sampled_2014_malware_api.csv` and returns `1` for malware, `0` for benign. Raises `ValueError` if neither token is found.
24	- `discover_dataset_files(data_dir: Path) -> list[Path]` — lists all `sampled_*_api.csv` files in `data_dir`.
25	- `load_single_file(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame` — reads one CSV, drops the first column, adds a `label` column from `extract_label_from_filename`, and adds a `year` column parsed from the filename.
26	- `load_year_data(data_dir: Path, year: int) -> pd.DataFrame` — loads and concatenates the benign and malware files for one year.
27	- `load_all_years(data_dir: Path) -> dict[int, pd.DataFrame]` — discovers every year present in `data_dir` and returns `{year: dataframe}` via `load_year_data`.
28	- `get_feature_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]` — returns all column names except `label` and `year`, used by every later step so the feature list is derived, not hard-coded.
29	
30	**Report:** `docs/step1_data_summary.md` — files loaded per year, shape after dropping the first column, malware/goodware counts per year, and any anomalies (missing files, unexpected row/column counts).
31	
32	**Testing:** tester can check `extract_label_from_filename` on known filenames, that `load_single_file` drops exactly one column and adds `label`/`year`, that `load_year_data` returns 3,000 rows (1,500 benign + 1,500 malware) with the expected number of feature columns, and that `load_all_years` returns one entry per year found in `input_data/`.
33	
34	## Step 2: Handle Data Drift
35	
36	**Approach:** Measure feature drift between years with the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, applied per feature between consecutive years and between the earliest and latest year. Rank features by KS statistic to find which drift most, and rank year-pairs by mean/max KS statistic to find which years differ most.
37	
38	**Files and functions (`src/drift_analysis.py`):**
39	- `ks_test_feature(series_a: pd.Series, series_b: pd.Series) -> tuple[float, float]` — runs `scipy.stats.ks_2samp`, returns `(statistic, p_value)` for one feature between two samples.
40	- `compute_drift_between_years(year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], year_a: int, year_b: int, feature_cols: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame` — applies `ks_test_feature` to every feature between the two years' dataframes, returns a dataframe indexed by feature with columns `statistic`, `p_value`.
41	- `compute_drift_across_years(year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], feature_cols: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame` — runs `compute_drift_between_years` on every consecutive year pair, returns one row per `(year_pair, feature, statistic, p_value)`.
42	- `compare_earliest_latest_year(year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], feature_cols: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame` — calls `compute_drift_between_years` on `(min(years), max(years))` specifically, giving the single comparison with the largest time gap, separately from the consecutive-year pairs above.
43	- `top_drifting_features(drift_df: pd.DataFrame, top_n: int = 20) -> pd.DataFrame` — sorts by `statistic` descending and returns the top-N rows.
44	- `most_different_year_pairs(drift_df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame` — groups `compute_drift_across_years` output by year pair, aggregates (mean and max statistic), sorted descending.
45	
46	**Report:** `docs/step2_drift_analysis.md` — method, table of top drifting features, which year pairs differ most, and what this implies for the models in later steps.
47	
48	**Testing:** tester can check `ks_test_feature` against two synthetic distributions with a known difference, that `compute_drift_between_years` returns one row per feature with statistics in `[0, 1]`, that `top_drifting_features` returns rows sorted descending by statistic, and that `compare_earliest_latest_year` picks the min and max year keys out of `year_data` rather than any other pair.
49	
50	## Step 3: Preprocess Data for Model Training
51	
52	**Approach:** Combine the per-year dataframes from Step 1 into a single training dataframe (train years) and a single test dataframe (test years), fit a `StandardScaler` on the training dataframe's features only, and transform both sets with it.
53	
54	**Files and functions (`src/preprocessing.py`):**
55	- `split_years_in_half(years: list[int]) -> tuple[list[int], list[int]]` — sorts the given years and splits them into `(train_years, test_years)` at the midpoint (earlier half trains, later half tests), so the primary split is always derived from whatever years are discovered rather than hard-coded.
56	- `split_by_year(year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], train_years: list[int], test_years: list[int]) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]` — concatenates the dataframes for `train_years` into one dataframe and for `test_years` into another; raises `ValueError` if a requested year is missing from `year_data`.
57	- `fit_scaler(train_df: pd.DataFrame, feature_cols: list[str]) -> StandardScaler` — fits a `StandardScaler` on `train_df[feature_cols]` only.
58	- `scale_features(df: pd.DataFrame, feature_cols: list[str], scaler: StandardScaler) -> np.ndarray` — transforms (never fits) using an already-fit scaler.
59	- `prepare_train_test(year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], feature_cols: list[str], train_years: list[int], test_years: list[int]) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, pd.Series, pd.Series, StandardScaler]` — runs `split_by_year`, `fit_scaler`, and `scale_features` and returns `X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, scaler`.
60	
61	No feature-selection step is included in this step (or anywhere in the plan) — see the note at the end of the leakage-prevention section above for why.
62	
63	**Report:** `docs/step3_preprocessing.md` — scaling method and confirmation it was fit on training years only, which years are train/test (and that they come from `split_years_in_half`, not a literal), how leakage is prevented (cross-referenced to the section above), and a note that feature selection is intentionally not used.
64	
65	**Testing:** tester can check that `split_years_in_half` divides a list of years into two halves of (near-)equal size with no overlap, that `split_by_year` raises on an unknown year, that the scaler's learned mean/scale come only from the training dataframe (e.g., compare `scaler.mean_` to a manually computed mean of just the training years), and that `prepare_train_test` output shapes match the row counts of the requested years.
66	
67	## Step 4: Apply Machine Learning Classifiers
68	
69	**Approach:** Train at least two scikit-learn classifiers — Logistic Regression (simple, interpretable linear baseline) and Random Forest (non-linear, handles the high-dimensional binary API-call features well) — on the Step 3 training data. All classifiers use `random_state=42` for reproducibility.
70	
71	**Files and functions (`src/models.py`):**
72	- `get_classifier_factories(random_state: int = 42) -> dict[str, Callable[[], object]]` — returns `{"logistic_regression": lambda: LogisticRegression(...), "random_forest": lambda: RandomForestClassifier(...)}`, i.e. zero-argument factories that each construct a fresh, unfitted classifier with fixed hyperparameters. This is the single source of truth for classifier hyperparameters; both `get_classifiers` and Step 7's `retraining_trajectory` build on it.
73	- `get_classifiers(random_state: int = 42) -> dict[str, object]` — calls every factory from `get_classifier_factories` once and returns `{name: classifier_instance}`, for callers (Steps 4-6) that only need one trained instance of each classifier and never need to reset it.
74	- `train_classifiers(classifiers: dict[str, object], X_train: np.ndarray, y_train: pd.Series) -> dict[str, object]` — calls `.fit()` on each classifier with the training data and returns the same dict with fitted models.
75	
76	**Report:** `docs/step4_models.md` — which classifiers, why, and a table of their hyperparameters (including `random_state`).
77	
78	**Testing:** tester can check `get_classifier_factories` returns at least two distinct, callable factories that each produce an unfitted estimator on every call (two calls to the same factory give `==`-equal but not identical, unfitted objects), that `get_classifiers` returns at least two distinct classifier types each using `random_state=42`, and that `train_classifiers` returns fitted estimators (e.g., `hasattr(model, "coef_")` or `"classes_"` present after fitting).
79	
80	## Step 5: Evaluate Classifier Performance
81	
82	**Approach:** Evaluate each trained classifier on the pooled test set (test years combined) using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, with malware (`label == 1`) as the positive class.
83	
84	**Files and functions (`src/evaluation.py`):**
85	- `evaluate_classifier(model: object, X_test: np.ndarray, y_test: pd.Series) -> dict[str, float]` — predicts on `X_test` and returns `{"accuracy": ..., "precision": ..., "recall": ..., "f1": ...}` computed with `pos_label=1`.
86	- `evaluate_all(models: dict[str, object], X_test: np.ndarray, y_test: pd.Series) -> pd.DataFrame` — runs `evaluate_classifier` for every model, returns one row per classifier.
87	
88	**Report:** `docs/step5_evaluation.md` — table of accuracy/precision/recall/F1 per classifier on the pooled test set, and observations about which classifier does better and why that might be.
89	
90	**Testing:** tester can check `evaluate_classifier` against a classifier with known predictions (e.g., a dummy classifier that always predicts 0) to confirm the metrics match a hand-computed value, and that `evaluate_all` returns one row per input classifier with all four metric columns.
91	
92	## Step 6: Test Data Prediction
93	
94	**Approach:** Reuse the trained classifiers from Step 4 and predict on each individual test year separately (not just the pooled test set), to see how performance changes as the gap between training years and the predicted year grows.
95	
96	**Files and functions (`src/evaluation.py`, extended):**
97	- `evaluate_by_year(models: dict[str, object], year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], feature_cols: list[str], scaler: StandardScaler, years: list[int]) -> pd.DataFrame` — for each year in `years`, scales that year's features with the already-fit `scaler` (never re-fit), predicts with each model, and returns one row per `(year, classifier)` with accuracy/precision/recall/F1.
98	
99	**Report:** `docs/step6_test_results.md` — table of year x classifier metrics, and a description of how performance changes as the data drifts further from the training years (2014-2017).
100	
101	**Testing:** tester can check `evaluate_by_year` returns one row per `(year, classifier)` combination for the requested years, that it never calls `.fit()` on the scaler (e.g., by asserting `scaler.mean_` is unchanged before/after the call), and that metrics are in `[0, 1]`.
102	
103	## Step 7: Sustainable ML Approach
104	
105	**Approach:** Compare two strategies across the test years (the later half from `split_years_in_half`) in chronological order, run separately for **both** classifiers from Step 4 (logistic regression and random forest) — neither is dropped, since Steps 5-6 evaluate both and Step 7 should show whether retraining helps each one:
106	1. **Static model:** trained once on `train_years`, never updated, evaluated on each test year as in Step 6.
107	2. **Periodic retraining:** after each test year is scored, that year's labeled data is added to the training pool and a *fresh* classifier (from `get_classifier_factories`, never the already-fitted Step 4 instance) is retrained before scoring the next year (e.g., score the first test year with the model trained on `train_years`, then retrain on `train_years + [first test year]` before scoring the second test year, and so on). Before each retrain, a **new `StandardScaler` is fit from scratch on the current (growing) training pool** — the scaler is not reused across rounds — because the drift motivating this step can shift feature means/scales too, and refitting still never touches the not-yet-scored year.
108	
109	This directly answers whether periodic retraining helps and avoids leakage, since a year is only added to the training pool (for both the classifier and the scaler) after it has been scored once as unseen data.
110	
111	**Files and functions (`src/sustainable.py`):**
112	- `static_model_trajectory(models: dict[str, object], year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], feature_cols: list[str], scaler: StandardScaler, test_years: list[int]) -> pd.DataFrame` — thin wrapper around `evaluate_by_year` representing the never-updated baseline for all classifiers in `models` at once (one row per `(year, classifier)`, matching `evaluate_by_year`'s output).
113	- `retraining_trajectory(classifier_factory: Callable[[], object], year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], feature_cols: list[str], train_years: list[int], test_years: list[int]) -> pd.DataFrame` — implements the year-by-year retrain loop described above for a **single** classifier factory (fitting a new scaler each round internally; no `scaler` parameter, since none is reused across rounds), returns one row per `(year, metric)` for that retrained model.
114	- `run_sustainability_comparison(classifier_factories: dict[str, Callable[[], object]], models: dict[str, object], year_data: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], feature_cols: list[str], scaler: StandardScaler, train_years: list[int], test_years: list[int]) -> pd.DataFrame` — loops `retraining_trajectory` over every entry in `classifier_factories` (i.e., both classifiers), calls `static_model_trajectory` once for the matching `models`, and concatenates everything into one table with a `classifier` column so both classifiers' static-vs-retrained comparisons are in a single dataframe.
115	- `compare_static_vs_retrained(static_df: pd.DataFrame, retrained_df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame` — merges the two trajectories into one table keyed by `(year, classifier)` for side-by-side comparison; used internally by `run_sustainability_comparison`.
116	
117	**Report:** `docs/step7_sustainable_approach.md` — the retraining approach tried, a table comparing it with the static model across test years **for both classifiers**, and conclusions for `REPORT.md`.
118	
119	**Testing:** tester can check `retraining_trajectory` grows its training set by one year after each scored year (e.g., by inspecting the size of the training data passed to each refit) and that each round's scaler is a distinct, newly-fit object (not the same instance reused), that `compare_static_vs_retrained` aligns rows by `(year, classifier)` without dropping or duplicating any test year, and that `run_sustainability_comparison`'s output contains both classifier names from `classifier_factories`.
120	
121	## Orchestration
122	
123	`src/main.py` — a `main() -> None` function (invoked by `python -m src.main`) that calls the functions above in order (load data -> drift analysis -> preprocess -> train -> evaluate -> evaluate by year -> sustainable comparison) and prints/saves the results used to fill in the `docs/` reports. No step's hard-coded assumptions (years present, number of classifiers, feature count) belong in `main.py`; those are all derived from `input_data/` and the dicts returned by the functions above.
124	
125	## Post Step 7: Project adjustments
126	
127	Steps 1-7 are implemented as library functions in `src/`, but no driver file
128	exists yet — there is nothing a grader or the live check-in can actually run
129	from the console to see the project work end to end. This section plans a
130	console driver that wires the existing Step 1-7 functions together and
131	exposes every one of them as a runnable action, without duplicating any of
132	their logic. This is a planning-only addition: no code is written under
133	this section; it describes what the builder will implement next.
134	
135	**Approach:** Split the driver into two new, decoupled modules so that
136	argument parsing (how the console is driven) stays independent of
137	orchestration (what each step does), matching the existing one-module-per-
138	concern layout of `src/`:
139	
140	- `src/cli.py` — owns the console interface only; knows nothing about
141	  pandas, scikit-learn, or any Step 1-7 function.
142	- `src/main.py` — owns orchestration only; calls the Step 1-7 functions
143	  already planned above (`data_loader`, `drift_analysis`, `preprocessing`,
144	  `models`, `evaluation`, `sustainable`) and formats their output for the
145	  console. `main.py` never parses `sys.argv` itself, so the two concerns
146	  can change independently (e.g. adding a new console flag never touches
147	  the orchestration code, and adding a new pipeline step never touches
148	  argument parsing).
149	
150	**Files and functions:**
151	
152	- `src/cli.py`:
153	  - `build_arg_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser` — defines one
154	    `argparse` parser with a `--data-dir` option (default `input_data`,
155	    so the dataset location is still determined at run time per AGENTS.md,
156	    never hard-coded) and a `--step` option restricted to
157	    `{"all", "load", "drift", "preprocess", "train", "evaluate",
158	    "evaluate-by-year", "sustainable"}` (default `"all"`), so every
159	    Step 1-7 function family is individually reachable from the console
160	    as well as runnable together.
161	  - `parse_args(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> argparse.Namespace` —
162	    thin wrapper around `build_arg_parser().parse_args(argv)`, kept
163	    separate so tests can call it directly with a list of strings instead
164	    of patching `sys.argv`.
165	- `src/main.py`:
166	  - `PipelineContext` (a small `dataclass`) — holds whatever state later
167	    steps need that earlier steps produced: `data_dir`, `year_data`,
168	    `feature_cols`, `train_years`, `test_years`, `X_train`, `X_test`,
169	    `y_train`, `y_test`, `scaler`, `classifiers`, `classifier_factories`.
170	    Fields start unset (`None`) and are filled in by the step-runner
171	    functions below, so each runner can check "has this already been
172	    computed by an earlier call?" instead of recomputing it.
173	  - `ensure_data_loaded(context: PipelineContext) -> None`,
174	    `ensure_preprocessed(context: PipelineContext) -> None`,
175	    `ensure_trained(context: PipelineContext) -> None` — each calls the
176	    relevant Step 1/3/4 functions (`load_all_years` + `get_feature_columns`
177	    + `split_years_in_half`; `prepare_train_test`; `get_classifiers` +
178	    `get_classifier_factories` + `train_classifiers`) only if the
179	    corresponding `PipelineContext` fields are still unset. This is what
180	    lets a console user request a single step (e.g. `--step sustainable`)
181	    and still get correct results, because the prerequisite steps it
182	    depends on run automatically and only once.
183	  - `run_step1_load(context) -> dict[int, pd.DataFrame]`,
184	    `run_step2_drift(context) -> pd.DataFrame`,
185	    `run_step3_preprocess(context) -> None`,
186	    `run_step4_train(context) -> dict[str, object]`,
187	    `run_step5_evaluate(context) -> pd.DataFrame`,
188	    `run_step6_evaluate_by_year(context) -> pd.DataFrame`,
189	    `run_step7_sustainable(context) -> pd.DataFrame` — one function per
190	    step, each calling `ensure_*` for whatever it needs first, then
191	    calling only the already-planned Step 1-7 functions (no new modeling
192	    or data logic lives here), and returning the dataframe/dict that step
193	    produces so it can be printed.
194	  - `format_dataframe_for_console(df: pd.DataFrame) -> str` — a single
195	    shared helper (so every step prints tables the same way) that calls
196	    `pandas.DataFrame.to_string(index=False)` and rounds floats for
197	    readability.
198	  - `run_selected_step(context, step: str) -> None` — maps the `--step`
199	    string from `parse_args` onto the `run_stepN_*` functions above
200	    (`"all"` runs all seven in order), printing each result with
201	    `format_dataframe_for_console`.
202	  - `main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None` — calls
203	    `parse_args(argv)`, builds a `PipelineContext` from `args.data_dir`,
204	    and calls `run_selected_step(context, args.step)`. This is the
205	    function `python -m src.main` invokes, keeping AGENTS.md's documented
206	    run command correct while adding the `--step` option as a console
207	    convenience, not a replacement for it (running with no arguments
208	    still runs everything, exactly as AGENTS.md describes today).
209	
210	**Why no new top-level folder:** results are printed to the console, not
211	written to a new `results/`-style folder, so this change needs no edit to
212	AGENTS.md's folder layout section.
213	
214	**Report:** `docs/post_step7_project_adjustments.md` — what was planned
215	here and why, written by the builder once this section existed (this
216	section is also referenced, not duplicated, by that report).
217	
218	**Testing:** once implemented, the tester can check that `parse_args`
219	rejects a `--step` value outside the fixed set, that each `ensure_*`
220	helper is a no-op (does not recompute) when its `PipelineContext` fields
221	are already set, that `run_selected_step(context, "all")` populates every
222	`PipelineContext` field exactly once even though multiple `run_stepN_*`
223	functions depend on the same prerequisite, and that `main([])` (no
224	arguments) runs the full pipeline, matching today's documented
225	`python -m src.main` behavior.

1	# Step 7 Review: Sustainable ML Approach (Post Step 7 plan + src/sustainable.py)
2	
3	- Reviewer transcript: transcripts/37_2026-11-01_reviewer_step7.md
4	- What was reviewed: PLAN.md at commit 8cb07f2 (especially the "Post Step 7: Project adjustments" section), and the code changes in `.harness/diffs/step7_diff.patch` (the diff from step7-start to commit 8cb07f2, i.e. `src/sustainable.py`), with `src/evaluation.py`, `src/preprocessing.py`, and `src/models.py` opened for context.
5	
6	## Comments (reviewer)
7	
8	| # | Severity | Location | Issue | Suggested fix |
9	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
10	| 1 | High | PLAN.md, "Post Step 7" section — `run_step1_load`, `run_step3_preprocess`, `run_step4_train` vs. `run_selected_step` / `format_dataframe_for_console` | The plan says `run_selected_step` prints "each result with `format_dataframe_for_console`", but `format_dataframe_for_console(df: pd.DataFrame) -> str` only accepts a single dataframe. `run_step1_load` is planned to return `dict[int, pd.DataFrame]` (one frame per year), `run_step4_train` returns `dict[str, object]` (fitted classifiers, not a frame), and `run_step3_preprocess` returns `None`. 1	"""Step 1: load the Android API-call dataset and attach labels/years.
2	
3	Reads the ``sampled_<year>_<class>_api.csv`` files from a data directory,
4	drops the identifier column, and attaches a binary ``label`` (1 = malware,
5	0 = benign) and an integer ``year`` column parsed from each filename. Years
6	and files present are discovered at runtime; nothing about the dataset is
7	hard-coded here.
8	"""
9	
10	import re
11	import warnings
12	from pathlib import Path
13	
14	import pandas as pd
15	
16	# Matches filenames like "sampled_2014_malware_api.csv" and captures the
17	# year and class-label token so both can be parsed in one place. Matched
18	# case-insensitively so this stays consistent with
19	# extract_label_from_filename, which also lowercases before matching.
20	_FILENAME_PATTERN = re.compile(r"sampled_(\d{4})_(benign|malware)_api\.csv$", re.IGNORECASE)
21	
22	# Expected shape (rows, columns) of a raw dataset file before the first
23	# column is dropped, per AGENTS.md/ASSIGNMENT.md. A column-count mismatch
24	# only triggers a warning (files are not rejected), but a row count above
25	# this is truncated to the expected row count (see load_single_file) so
26	# every file contributes the documented sample size.
27	_EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE = (1500, 1849)
28	
29	
30	def extract_label_from_filename(filename: str) -> int:
31	    """Parse the binary label out of a dataset filename.
32	
33	    Args:
34	        filename: A filename such as "sampled_2014_malware_api.csv". Only
35	            the "benign" or "malware" token is required to be present;
36	            the full naming scheme is not enforced here.
37	
38	    Returns:
39	        1 if the filename contains "malware", 0 if it contains "benign".
40	
41	    Raises:
42	        ValueError: If neither "benign" nor "malware" appears in filename.
43	    """
44	    name = Path(filename).name.lower()
45	    if "malware" in name:
46	        return 1
47	    if "benign" in name:
48	        return 0
49	    raise ValueError(
50	        f"Could not find 'benign' or 'malware' token in filename: {filename}"
51	    )
52	
53	
54	def _extract_year_from_filename(filename: str) -> int:
55	    """Parse the four-digit year out of a dataset filename.
56	
57	    Args:
58	        filename: A filename such as "sampled_2014_malware_api.csv".
59	
60	    Returns:
61	        The year as an int.
62	
63	    Raises:
64	        ValueError: If the filename does not match the expected
65	            "sampled_<year>_<class>_api.csv" naming scheme.
66	    """
67	    match = _FILENAME_PATTERN.match(Path(filename).name)
68	    if not match:
69	        raise ValueError(
70	            f"Filename does not match 'sampled_<year>_<benign|malware>_api.csv': "
71	            f"{filename}"
72	        )
73	    return int(match.group(1))
74	
75	
76	def discover_dataset_files(data_dir: Path) -> list[Path]:
77	    """List all dataset CSV files present in a directory.
78	
79	    Args:
80	        data_dir: Directory to search, e.g. the project's input_data/.
81	
82	    Returns:
83	        A sorted list of paths matching "sampled_*_api.csv", so the set of
84	        files (and therefore years/classes) is determined at run time
85	        rather than assumed in advance.
86	    """
87	    return sorted(Path(data_dir).glob("sampled_*_api.csv"))
88	
89	
90	def load_single_file(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
91	    """Load one dataset CSV file and attach its label and year.
92	
93	    Drops the first column (an app identifier, not a feature) and adds a
94	    `label` column (from the filename's benign/malware token) and a `year`
95	    column (from the filename's year token).
96	
97	    Args:
98	        path: Path to a single "sampled_<year>_<class>_api.csv" file.
99	
100	    Returns:
101	        A dataframe with the identifier column removed and `label`/`year`
102	        columns appended to the original API-call feature columns.
103	    """
104	    df = pd.read_csv(path)
105	    # Flag unexpected shapes (e.g. a differently-sampled file) before the
106	    # first column is dropped, so anomalies surface automatically instead
107	    # of relying on manual inspection when writing docs/step1_data_summary.md.
108	    if df.shape != _EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE:
109	        warnings.warn(
110	            f"{path.name}: expected raw shape {_EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE}, got {df.shape}",
111	            stacklevel=2,
112	        )
113	    # Some real files (2014-2018) contain more rows than AGENTS.md's stated
114	    # 1,500 per file. Take the first N rows deterministically so every file
115	    # contributes the documented sample size instead of over-representing
116	    # years that happen to have extra rows.
117	    expected_rows = _EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE[0]
118	    if len(df) > expected_rows:
119	        df = df.iloc[:expected_rows].reset_index(drop=True)
120	    # The first column is an app identifier (e.g. "apkname"), not a feature.
121	    df = df.drop(columns=df.columns[0])
122	    # label/year are added below; if either name already exists among the
123	    # feature columns, assign() would silently overwrite it and
124	    # get_feature_columns would then silently lose a real feature.
125	    collisions = {"label", "year"} & set(df.columns)
126	    if collisions:
127	        raise ValueError(
128	            f"{path.name}: feature column(s) {sorted(collisions)} collide with "
129	            "reserved 'label'/'year' column names"
130	        )
131	    # Assign both columns together (rather than one at a time) to avoid
132	    # repeated in-place inserts on a wide dataframe.
133	    return df.assign(
134	        label=extract_label_from_filename(path.name),
135	        year=_extract_year_from_filename(path.name),
136	    )
137	
138	
139	def load_year_data(data_dir: Path, year: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
140	    """Load and combine the benign and malware files for a single year.
141	
142	    Args:
143	        data_dir: Directory containing the dataset CSV files.
144	        year: The year to load, e.g. 2014.
145	
146	    Returns:
147	        A dataframe combining that year's benign and malware rows.
148	
149	    Raises:
150	        FileNotFoundError: If either the benign or malware file for `year`
151	            is missing from `data_dir`.
152	    """
153	    data_dir = Path(data_dir)
154	    class_files = {
155	        "benign": data_dir / f"sampled_{year}_benign_api.csv",
156	        "malware": data_dir / f"sampled_{year}_malware_api.csv",
157	    }
158	    frames = []
159	    for class_name, file_path in class_files.items():
160	        if not file_path.exists():
161	            raise FileNotFoundError(
162	                f"Missing {class_name} file for year {year}: {file_path}"
163	            )
164	        frames.append(load_single_file(file_path))
165	    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
166	
167	
168	def load_all_years(data_dir: Path) -> dict[int, pd.DataFrame]:
169	    """Discover and load every year present in a data directory.
170	
171	    Args:
172	        data_dir: Directory containing the dataset CSV files.
173	
174	    Returns:
175	        A dict mapping each discovered year to its combined
176	        (benign + malware) dataframe, as produced by `load_year_data`.
177	    """
178	    data_dir = Path(data_dir)
179	    years = sorted({_extract_year_from_filename(p.name) for p in discover_dataset_files(data_dir)})
180	    return {year: load_year_data(data_dir, year) for year in years}
181	
182	
183	def get_feature_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]:
184	    """Return the API-call feature column names of a loaded dataframe.
185	
186	    Excludes the `label` and `year` columns added during loading, so later
187	    steps always derive the feature list from the data rather than
188	    hard-coding it.
189	
190	    Args:
191	        df: A dataframe produced by `load_single_file`/`load_year_data`/
192	            `load_all_years`.
193	
194	    Returns:
195	        The list of feature column names, in their original order.
196	    """
197	    return [col for col in df.columns if col not in ("label", "year")]
198

# column is dropped, per AGENTS.md/ASSIGNMENT.md. A column-count mismatch
# only triggers a warning (files are not rejected), but a row count above
# this is truncated to the expected row count (see load_single_file) so
# every file contributes the documented sample size.
_EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE = (1500, 1849)


def extract_label_from_filename(filename: str) -> int:
    """Parse the binary label out of a dataset filename.

    Args:
        filename: A filename such as "sampled_2014_malware_api.csv". Only
            the "benign" or "malware" token is required to be present;
            the full naming scheme is not enforced here.

    Returns:
        1 if the filename contains "malware", 0 if it contains "benign".

    Raises:
        ValueError: If neither "benign" nor "malware" appears in filename.
    """
    name = Path(filename).name.lower()
    if "malware" in name:
        return 1
    if "benign" in name:
        return 0
    raise ValueError(
        f"Could not find 'benign' or 'malware' token in filename: {filename}"
    )


def _extract_year_from_filename(filename: str) -> int:
    """Parse the four-digit year out of a dataset filename.

    Args:
        filename: A filename such as "sampled_2014_malware_api.csv".

    Returns:
        The year as an int.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the filename does not match the expected
            "sampled_<year>_<class>_api.csv" naming scheme.
    """
    match = _FILENAME_PATTERN.match(Path(filename).name)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Filename does not match 'sampled_<year>_<benign|malware>_api.csv': "
            f"{filename}"
        )
    return int(match.group(1))


def discover_dataset_files(data_dir: Path) -> list[Path]:
    """List all dataset CSV files present in a directory.

    Args:
        data_dir: Directory to search, e.g. the project's input_data/.

    Returns:
        A sorted list of paths matching "sampled_*_api.csv", so the set of
        files (and therefore years/classes) is determined at run time
        rather than assumed in advance.
    """
    return sorted(Path(data_dir).glob("sampled_*_api.csv"))


def load_single_file(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load one dataset CSV file and attach its label and year.

    Drops the first column (an app identifier, not a feature) and adds a
    `label` column (from the filename's benign/malware token) and a `year`
    column (from the filename's year token).

    Args:
        path: Path to a single "sampled_<year>_<class>_api.csv" file.

    Returns:
        A dataframe with the identifier column removed and `label`/`year`
        columns appended to the original API-call feature columns.
    """
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    # Flag unexpected shapes (e.g. a differently-sampled file) before the
    # first column is dropped, so anomalies surface automatically instead
    # of relying on manual inspection when writing docs/step1_data_summary.md.
    if df.shape != _EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE:
        warnings.warn(
            f"{path.name}: expected raw shape {_EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE}, got {df.shape}",
            stacklevel=2,
        )
    # Some real files (2014-2018) contain more rows than AGENTS.md's stated
    # 1,500 per file. Take the first N rows deterministically so every file
    # contributes the documented sample size instead of over-representing
    # years that happen to have extra rows.
    expected_rows = _EXPECTED_RAW_SHAPE[0]
    if len(df) > expected_rows:
        df = df.iloc[:expected_rows].reset_index(drop=True)
    # The first column is an app identifier (e.g. "apkname"), not a feature.
    df = df.drop(columns=df.columns[0])
    # label/year are added below; if either name already exists among the
    # feature columns, assign() would silently overwrite it and
    # get_feature_columns would then silently lose a real feature.
    collisions = {"label", "year"} & set(df.columns)
    if collisions:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{path.name}: feature column(s) {sorted(collisions)} collide with "
            "reserved 'label'/'year' column names"
        )
    # Assign both columns together (rather than one at a time) to avoid
    # repeated in-place inserts on a wide dataframe.
    return df.assign(
        label=extract_label_from_filename(path.name),
        year=_extract_year_from_filename(path.name),
    )


def load_year_data(data_dir: Path, year: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load and combine the benign and malware files for a single year.

    Args:
        data_dir: Directory containing the dataset CSV files.
        year: The year to load, e.g. 2014.

    Returns:
        A dataframe combining that year's benign and malware rows.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: If either the benign or malware file for `year`
            is missing from `data_dir`.
    """
    data_dir = Path(data_dir)
    class_files = {
        "benign": data_dir / f"sampled_{year}_benign_api.csv",
        "malware": data_dir / f"sampled_{year}_malware_api.csv",
    }
    frames = []
    for class_name, file_path in class_files.items():
        if not file_path.exists():
            raise FileNotFoundError(
                f"Missing {class_name} file for year {year}: {file_path}"
            )
        frames.append(load_single_file(file_path))
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)


def load_all_years(data_dir: Path) -> dict[int, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Discover and load every year present in a data directory.

    Args:
        data_dir: Directory containing the dataset CSV files.

    Returns:
        A dict mapping each discovered year to its combined
        (benign + malware) dataframe, as produced by `load_year_data`.
    """
    data_dir = Path(data_dir)
    years = sorted({_extract_year_from_filename(p.name) for p in discover_dataset_files(data_dir)})
    return {year: load_year_data(data_dir, year) for year in years}


def get_feature_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]:
    """Return the API-call feature column names of a loaded dataframe.

    Excludes the `label` and `year` columns added during loading, so later
    steps always derive the feature list from the data rather than
    hard-coding it.

    Args:
        df: A dataframe produced by `load_single_file`/`load_year_data`/
            `load_all_years`.

    Returns:
        The list of feature column names, in their original order.
    """
    return [col for col in df.columns if col not in ("label", "year")]

# Post Step 7 Report: Project Adjustments

Written by the builder agent.

- Builder transcript: transcripts/36_2026-11-01_builder_step7.md
- What this covers: a planning-only addition to `PLAN.md` (section "Post
  Step 7: Project adjustments") for a console driver that exposes all of
  Steps 1-7. No code was written in this session; this report records what
  was planned and why, for the builder session that implements it next.

## Why this was needed

AGENTS.md documents `python -m src.main` as the way to run the project, but
no `src/main.py` exists yet — `src/` only has the Step 1-7 library modules
(`data_loader.py`, `drift_analysis.py`, `preprocessing.py`, `models.py`,
`evaluation.py`, `sustainable.py`). There was nothing a grader, or the
instructor during the live check-in, could actually run from the console
to see the project work end to end, or to re-run a single step (e.g. just
the drift analysis, or just the sustainability comparison) without writing
a one-off script. The task was to close that gap at the planning level
first, so the next builder session has an unambiguous spec to implement
against.

## Decisions and reasoning

| # | Decision | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Split the driver into two new modules, `src/cli.py` (argument parsing) and `src/main.py` (orchestration), instead of one file. | AGENTS.md requires code to be "decoupled and modular" and that "changing one thing should generally not cause more changes to occur whenever possible." Argument parsing and pipeline orchestration are the two concerns a driver has; keeping them in separate modules means adding a console flag later never touches orchestration code, and adding a new pipeline step never touches argument parsing. |
| 2 | Add a `--step` option (`all`, `load`, `drift`, `preprocess`, `train`, `evaluate`, `evaluate-by-year`, `sustainable`) rather than only a no-argument "run everything" mode. | The task requires that "all necessary functions of the program should be accessible/implemented in this driver," not just the full pipeline. A single flag with one value per Step 1-7 function family satisfies that without growing into a large set of separate scripts. |
| 3 | Introduce a `PipelineContext` dataclass with `ensure_*` helper functions that compute a prerequisite only if it is not already set, instead of requiring the console user to run earlier steps first. | Later steps depend on earlier steps' outputs (e.g. Step 7's sustainability comparison needs the Step 3 scaler and Step 4 classifiers). Without this, `--step sustainable` alone would either crash or silently skip the dependency. The `ensure_*` pattern makes every step independently runnable while computing each prerequisite at most once, which also keeps the plan testable (a test can assert an `ensure_*` call is a no-op the second time). |
| 4 | Keep `python -m src.main` with no arguments running the full pipeline, matching what AGENTS.md already documents, rather than changing the default behavior. | AGENTS.md is the shared context file all three agents (and the grader) rely on for "how to run the code." Changing the no-argument behavior would silently invalidate that documentation; defaulting `--step` to `"all"` keeps the documented command correct while still adding the new capability. |
| 5 | Do not introduce a new `results/`-style folder for saving CSV output; print formatted tables to the console instead. | The task specifically asks for a program that "run[s] in the console." Writing output files would also require editing AGENTS.md's folder layout section, which is out of scope for a planning-only task — printing keeps this adjustment self-contained to `PLAN.md` and the new `src/` modules. |
| 6 | Write no code in this session; only add a PLAN.md section and this report. | Explicitly required by the task instructions for this session. The plan is detailed enough (function names, signatures, and responsibilities) that a later builder session can implement it without re-deriving the design. |

## What was changed

- `PLAN.md`: added a new "Post Step 7: Project adjustments" section
  describing `src/cli.py` and `src/main.py` — their functions, signatures,
  and responsibilities — and why no new top-level folder is needed.
  Commit: `47a20fd`.
- `docs/post_step7_project_adjustments.md` (this file): recorded the
  reasoning above. Commit: see below.

Not applicable to this session: no code was written or run, only `PLAN.md`
prose and this report. The next builder session that implements
`src/cli.py` and `src/main.py` will need to verify the driver against the
existing Step 1-7 functions and the tester's forthcoming tests for this
section.
